questions.question_stem: Why are permissionless blockchains best described as a dual-use environment rather than as simply anonymous criminal infrastructure?
questions.correct_answer: They allow open, borderless access that illicit actors can exploit, while public ledgers also preserve evidence investigators can later analyze.
incorrect_answers: They provide pseudonymous access but require most users to pass exchange-style KYC before wallet-to-wallet transfers can settle on-chain globally.
They attract illicit use mainly because privacy coins dominate public-chain payments, while ordinary ledgers rarely produce useful evidence.
They become risky mostly when centralized services ignore AML duties, while base-layer openness plays only a secondary role in illicit use.
questions.explanation: The lesson's core framing is dual-use: weak base-layer identity checks and borderless settlement create risk, but immutable public records create durable forensic traces.

questions.question_stem: An investigator can see that one wallet cluster repeatedly receives ransomware proceeds, but has not yet linked the cluster to a person. Which concept best describes that situation?
questions.correct_answer: Pseudonymity: the address activity is persistent and traceable, but real-world attribution still requires additional evidence.
incorrect_answers: Anonymity: the cluster can receive funds without an identity field, so analysts should treat all of its later spends as untraceable.
Attribution: recurring ransomware deposits are enough to assign the cluster to a named operator before off-chain corroboration.
Service clustering: repeated receipts show the cluster is a regulated exchange account rather than an offender-controlled wallet.
questions.explanation: Pseudonymous addresses can be tracked over time without automatically identifying a human operator. Attribution often needs exchange records, OSINT, subpoenas, seized devices, or other off-chain evidence.

questions.question_stem: A laundering path splits a large payment into many smaller transfers, routes some value through a mixer, and swaps the rest through a bridge into another asset. What is the best forensic interpretation?
questions.correct_answer: The actor is combining techniques that blur source, volume, and cross-chain continuity rather than relying on one method to erase the ledger.
incorrect_answers: The actor is relying on the bridge as the main source of anonymity, so mixer timing and split-transfer patterns add little to the analysis.
The actor is using peel-chain style splitting to avoid exchange limits, so cross-chain correlation is unnecessary once value changes assets.
The actor is creating a path that can be resolved by following each output separately, without comparing timing or fee-adjusted amounts.
questions.explanation: Mixers, peel chains, layering, and chain hopping target different parts of the trail. They complicate source, path, volume, and continuity analysis, but do not delete historical ledger records.

questions.question_stem: A tracing team has a clean transaction graph showing funds moving from a theft address to an exchange deposit address. What would most directly move the investigation from tracing toward enforceable action?
questions.correct_answer: Exchange records, legal process, or other off-chain evidence that links the deposit account to an identity or controllable asset.
incorrect_answers: A more detailed analytics graph that scores the exchange deposit as high risk but does not identify the customer account.
An address-cluster label shared with partner agencies but not corroborated by records tying the label to a person or service account.
A report that the funds later moved to another chain, without a jurisdictional hook or account where assets can be frozen.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that transaction traces become seizures, prosecutions, sanctions, or freezes only when combined with attribution, legal authority, jurisdiction, and sometimes key or account control.

questions.question_stem: Why can a CoinJoin-style transaction undermine a common-input-ownership heuristic?
questions.correct_answer: Multiple users may intentionally contribute inputs to one transaction, so shared inputs do not necessarily mean one owner controls all of them.
incorrect_answers: The transaction is usually run by a custodial mixer, so all inputs should be attributed to the coordinator rather than the contributors.
The equal-sized outputs remove the need for input analysis, so investigators can infer one owner from the matching denominations.
The heuristic is designed only for exchange deposit addresses, so a CoinJoin transaction falls outside the model regardless of ownership.
questions.explanation: Forensic heuristics are useful but fallible inference rules. Privacy tools can deliberately target those assumptions, creating false-positive risks if heuristics are treated as proof.

questions.question_stem: Which comparison best captures the distinction between centralized exchanges, DEXs, and bridges in laundering workflows?
questions.correct_answer: Centralized exchanges can create KYC and fiat off-ramp records, DEXs automate crypto-to-crypto swaps, and bridges move value across chain boundaries that require correlation.
incorrect_answers: Centralized exchanges and DEXs both swap assets, but only DEXs routinely bind trades to verified customers while bridges add liquidity within one chain rather than crossing ledgers.
Centralized exchanges are mainly obfuscation tools, DEXs are regulated fiat cash-out ramps, and bridges give every route one shared identifier for investigators.
Centralized exchanges matter only after fiat cash-out, DEXs provide stronger anonymity than privacy coins, and bridges preserve one address across chains during laundering.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes chokepoints and trace surfaces: centralized exchanges may connect to accounts and fiat, DEXs reduce account-based intermediaries for crypto swaps, and bridges create cross-chain continuity challenges.

questions.question_stem: A bridge emits a withdrawal on Chain B minutes after a deposit on Chain A, with a fee-adjusted amount that closely matches the original transfer. Why is that useful for cross-chain tracing, and what remains unresolved?
questions.correct_answer: Bridge logs, timing, amount, and fee-adjusted matching can support transaction linkage across chains, but real-world identity attribution still needs corroborating evidence.
incorrect_answers: The match is enough to identify common ownership of both wallets, but investigators still need the bridge's pricing formula to value the transfer and allocate fees.
It shows a likely bridge interaction, but once value exits on Chain B analysts should stop using timing, amount, and bridge-log correlations for attribution.
It mainly proves the bridge was a regulated exchange deposit with customer records, while the unresolved issue is whether public ledgers recorded enough evidence for attribution review.
questions.explanation: The XSema-style slide supports automated cross-chain linkage from bridge logs, timing windows, and fee-adjusted amount matching. Separate attribution evidence is still needed before tying that linked flow to a human or organization.

questions.question_stem: A proposed provenance-bearing chain would require valid custody proofs before accepting transfers. Which evaluation best captures the design tradeoff involved?
questions.correct_answer: It could improve auditability and compliance, but it would reduce privacy and permissionless access while adding consensus-enforced public-protocol constraints.
incorrect_answers: It would improve privacy because only validated custody histories are visible, but it would weaken auditability by moving provenance outside consensus for most users.
It would help forensic review mainly by replacing legal process with protocol-level judgments about guilt, while preserving permissionless access.
It would address bridge thefts by making validator keys unnecessary, but leave privacy and compliance tradeoffs mostly unchanged for public-chain users.
questions.explanation: Embedded provenance can attach origin, custody, and compliance context to transactions, but the visible slides frame that as a public-protocol tradeoff involving auditability, privacy, permissionless access, and consensus enforcement.

questions.question_stem: In the Colonial Pipeline case, why was following the ransom trail not enough by itself to recover funds?
questions.correct_answer: Recovery required tracing to intersect with jurisdiction, legal authority, and control over the relevant key or account.
incorrect_answers: Recovery required a clean chain-of-custody graph, because a certain trace gives law enforcement control over the attacker's wallet.
Recovery depended on funds reaching a compliant fiat off-ramp, because warrants cannot affect assets before exchange deposit.
Recovery was limited because Bitcoin transactions are shielded from graph analysis, so agents relied only on victim records.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses Colonial Pipeline to distinguish tracing from recovery: live transaction visibility mattered, but asset recovery depended on legal process and practical control.

questions.question_stem: Under FinCEN's 2013 guidance, which actor is most likely to be treated as a money services business rather than an ordinary user?
questions.correct_answer: A business that accepts, transmits, buys, or sells convertible virtual currency for customers.
incorrect_answers: A person who buys virtual currency for personal purchases and uses it to pay merchants directly.
A noncustodial wallet developer who publishes code but does not control customer assets or transfers.
A merchant who accepts virtual currency for retail sales and later converts receipts at an exchange.
questions.explanation: The CRS reading emphasizes FinCEN's functional distinction: ordinary users are generally not MSBs, while administrators and exchangers operating as businesses may be money transmitters.

questions.question_stem: AML compliance can be understood as an institutional data-production system. Which scenario best illustrates that mechanism?
questions.correct_answer: An exchange maintains customer records, monitors suspicious behavior, and files reports that investigators can later use with transaction traces.
incorrect_answers: A blockchain analytics company publishes address risk scores, but no covered institution collects customer records or files reports.
A decentralized protocol lets users swap assets through smart contracts, so compliance data depends mainly on public transaction events.
A court treats virtual currency as funds in a criminal case, but the case does not involve institutional monitoring or reporting duties.
questions.explanation: The CRS report explains that covered institutions have AML programs, recordkeeping, and suspicious activity reporting duties. Those duties create off-chain evidence that can connect to pseudonymous flows.

questions.question_stem: Which policy argument best reflects the legal uncertainty around virtual currency regulation?
questions.correct_answer: Clearer AML coverage can help enforcement, but broad or unclear duties may burden legitimate developers and noncustodial actors who do not control customer funds.
incorrect_answers: AML duties should attach to wallet software, validators, and noncustodial developers because uncertainty mostly protects criminals from court jurisdiction in practice.
Virtual currencies fall outside existing AML law unless Congress creates a crypto-specific statute, so agencies should delay enforcement against exchangers and processors.
Safe harbors should exempt custodial exchanges from suspicious-report and registration duties because innovation concerns outweigh customer records.
questions.explanation: The CRS reading presents a tradeoff: regulators and prosecutors need workable legal categories, while overly broad obligations can chill innovation or sweep in actors without customer custody or control.
